title: Phase Transformation Mechanisms and Plastic Deformation in Shocked High-Pressure Minerals Using Near-Axis TKD and 4D-STEM
content: The Earth’s mantle transition zone (MTZ, 410-660 km depth) is bound by high-pressure mineral phase transitions and plays a crucial role in geodynamics at the interface between the upper to lower mantle. Based on laboratory experiments and global seismic studies, olivine, (Mg,Fe)2SiO₄, transforms into wadsleyite (wds) at ∼410 km depth and subsequently to the spinel-structured ringwoodite (rwd) at ∼520 km before breaking down to MgSiO3 + MgO at 660 km. These phase transitions influence mantle convection, subducting slab rheology, and are thought to contribute to the generation of deep-focus earthquakes [1, 2]. Understanding the phase transformation mechanisms, orientation relationships, and deformation behavior of these high-pressure minerals is critical for accurately modeling these dynamic and destructive processes. These transformations are known to occur both over geological timescales in the mantle and under rapid pressure-temperature-time (PTT) conditions in shocked meteorites, providing a unique natural laboratory for studying high-pressure mineral stability and deformation processes. However, accurately distinguishing wds from rwd in shocked meteorites remains a challenge due to their similar crystallographic structures, fine grain size, and extreme lattice distortions caused by high dislocation densities, stacking faults, and potential amorphization at grain boundaries.
